title: USPS Issues Diwali Forever Stamp With Houston Artist's Rangoli
excerpt: Sangita Bhutada's eight-foot rangoli anchors America's second Diwali stamp, issued October 21 in Washington with a 20 million print run.
body:
• The US Postal Service has issued its second-ever Diwali Forever stamp, dedicated on October 21, 2026 at the Embassy of India in Washington, DC, a decade after the first in 2016.
  • The stamp reproduces an eight-foot rangoli created by India-born, Houston-area artist Sangita Bhutada, who has practised the folk art for nearly 30 years; the original took eight to 10 days to make.
  • USPS printed 20 million stamps, sold in panes of 20 at 82 cents each ($16.40 a sheet) through post offices and the USPS Postal Store.
  • As a Forever stamp it stays valid for a one-ounce First-Class letter even if postal rates rise — diaspora families can use it for Diwali cards this season, with the festival's main day on November 8, 2026.

The United States Postal Service has issued a new Forever stamp celebrating Diwali, featuring a rangoli created by Indian artist Sangita Bhutada, according to the USPS announcement. The stamp was dedicated on October 21 at the Embassy of India in Washington, DC, in the presence of India's Ambassador to the US, Vinay Kwatra, and USPS senior vice-president Shibani Gambhir. It is only the second Diwali stamp USPS has issued; the first, featuring a diya, came in 2016.

An eight-foot rangoli, shrunk to a stamp

Bhutada, a native of India and longtime resident of the Houston area, has been a practitioner of rangoli — the traditional floor art made with coloured rice powder, chalk and flower petals — for nearly 30 years. For the stamp she created an original work eight feet in diameter, in blue, orange, green, red and white using starch-based coloured powder and coloured sand, set against a purple background. The piece took eight to 10 days to complete, far longer than the four to six hours she normally spends on a rangoli, so that it would photograph in high resolution.

https://x.com/adaderana/status/2118230647491997774

Houston-area photographer Bijay Dixit photographed the finished rangoli. Jennifer Arnold designed the stamp and William J. Gicker served as art director.

How to get it

USPS printed 20 million of the stamps. They are sold in panes of 20 at post offices nationwide and through the Postal Store, priced at the Forever rate of 82 cents per stamp. Because it is a Forever stamp, it will always be equal in value to the current First-Class Mail one-ounce price, regardless of future rate increases.

Why it lands with the diaspora

Diwali's main day this year falls on November 8, 2026, and the stamp arrives in time for the season's cards and gifts. For Indian American families, a federal stamp carrying a rangoli — an art form many grew up watching being drawn at the front door — is a small but visible piece of recognition, ten years after USPS first honoured the festival.

A decade between stamps

The 2016 first Diwali stamp featured a traditional diya, the oil lamp lit for the festival. This year's design moves from the lamp to the floor art that surrounds it. The dedication ceremony at the Embassy of India brought together diplomats, senior USPS officials and members of the Indian American community. The US Embassy in India also highlighted the stamp in a post on X on Thursday, the day the Times of India reported the issue to Indian readers.
